claim: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency is believed to confer protection against Plasmodium falciparum malaria.
source: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency is believed to confer protection against Plasmodium falciparum malaria, but the precise nature of the protective effect has proved difficult to define as G6PD deficiency has multiple allelic variants with different effects in males and females, and it has heterogeneous effects on the clinical outcome of P. falciparum infection.
evidence: This is a widely accepted hypothesis in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: G6PD deficiency has multiple allelic variants with different effects in males and females.
source: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency is believed to confer protection against Plasmodium falciparum malaria, but the precise nature of the protective effect has proved difficult to define as G6PD deficiency has multiple allelic variants with different effects in males and females, and it has heterogeneous effects on the clinical outcome of P. falciparum infection.
evidence: This is established knowledge about G6PD deficiency and is supported by the WHO classification system described in the manuscript.

claim: G6PD deficiency has heterogeneous effects on the clinical outcome of P. falciparum infection.
source: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency is believed to confer protection against Plasmodium falciparum malaria, but the precise nature of the protective effect has proved difficult to define as G6PD deficiency has multiple allelic variants with different effects in males and females, and it has heterogeneous effects on the clinical outcome of P. falciparum infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the manuscript showing different effects on cerebral malaria versus severe malarial anaemia.

claim: Increasing levels of G6PD deficiency are associated with decreasing risk of cerebral malaria.
source: Aggregated across all genotypes, we find that increasing levels of G6PD deficiency are associated with decreasing risk of cerebral malaria, but with increased risk of severe malarial anaemia.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by statistical analysis of the data presented in Tables 3, 6 and Figure 2.

claim: Increasing levels of G6PD deficiency are associated with increased risk of severe malarial anaemia.
source: Aggregated across all genotypes, we find that increasing levels of G6PD deficiency are associated with decreasing risk of cerebral malaria, but with increased risk of severe malarial anaemia.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by statistical analysis of the data presented in Tables 3, 6 and Figure 2.

claim: An evolutionary trade-off between different clinical outcomes of P. falciparum infection could have been a major cause of the high levels of G6PD polymorphism seen in human populations.
source: Models of balancing selection based on these findings indicate that an evolutionary trade-off between different clinical outcomes of P. falciparum infection could have been a major cause of the high levels of G6PD polymorphism seen in human populations.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the evolutionary modeling presented in the manuscript (Figures 3 and 4).

claim: G6PD is encoded by the G6PD gene on chromosome X.
source: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD), encoded by the G6PD gene on chromosome X, is an enzyme that acts to control oxidative damage in red blood cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the G6PD gene.

claim: G6PD is an enzyme that acts to control oxidative damage in red blood cells.
source: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD), encoded by the G6PD gene on chromosome X, is an enzyme that acts to control oxidative damage in red blood cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about G6PD function.

claim: G6PD deficiency is a common human genetic condition with many allelic variants causing different levels of enzyme deficiency.
source: G6PD deficiency is a common human genetic condition with many allelic variants causing different levels of enzyme deficiency, so that in some individuals it is asymptomatic whereas in others it can cause severe haemolytic anaemia (Beutler, 1994; Beutler and Vulliamy, 2002; Beutler, 2008; Minucci et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: In some individuals G6PD deficiency is asymptomatic whereas in others it can cause severe haemolytic anaemia.
source: G6PD deficiency is a common human genetic condition with many allelic variants causing different levels of enzyme deficiency, so that in some individuals it is asymptomatic whereas in others it can cause severe haemolytic anaemia (Beutler, 1994; Beutler and Vulliamy, 2002; Beutler, 2008; Minucci et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: The geographical distribution of G6PD deficiency corresponds to regions of the world where malaria is endemic, or has been in the relatively recent past.
source: The geographical distribution of G6PD deficiency corresponds to regions of the world where malaria is endemic, or has been in the relatively recent past, and it has been estimated that approximately 350 million people living in malaria-endemic countries are affected (Allison, 1960; Motulsky, 1960; Howes et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Approximately 350 million people living in malaria-endemic countries are affected by G6PD deficiency.
source: The geographical distribution of G6PD deficiency corresponds to regions of the world where malaria is endemic, or has been in the relatively recent past, and it has been estimated that approximately 350 million people living in malaria-endemic countries are affected (Allison, 1960; Motulsky, 1960; Howes et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: G6PD deficiency has risen to high frequency in malaria-endemic regions because it confers some level of resistance to malaria.
source: It was proposed over half a century ago, and is now widely accepted, that G6PD deficiency has risen to high frequency in malaria-endemic regions because it confers some level of resistance to malaria (Allison, 1960; Luzzatto, 2015).
evidence: This is a widely accepted hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: Haplotype and sequence analyses indicate that G6PD variants have evolved independently, at a frequency that is inconsistent with random genetic drift.
source: Evolutionary support for this hypothesis is provided by haplotype and sequence analyses indicating that G6PD variants have evolved independently, at a frequency that is inconsistent with random genetic drift, and over a period of time that is consistent with the estimated time since the emergence of malaria (Tishkoff et al., 2001; Sabeti et al., 2002; Saunders et al., 2002; Verrelli et al., 2002; Saunders et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to evolutionary studies.

claim: G6PD variants have evolved over a period of time that is consistent with the estimated time since the emergence of malaria.
source: Evolutionary support for this hypothesis is provided by haplotype and sequence analyses indicating that G6PD variants have evolved independently, at a frequency that is inconsistent with random genetic drift, and over a period of time that is consistent with the estimated time since the emergence of malaria (Tishkoff et al., 2001; Sabeti et al., 2002; Saunders et al., 2002; Verrelli et al., 2002; Saunders et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to evolutionary studies.

claim: An early study concluded that G6PD deficiency protects against P. falciparum malaria in heterozygous females.
source: An early study concluded that G6PD deficiency protects against P. falciparum malaria in heterozygous females (Bienzle et al., 1972) and this is supported by a number of more recent studies (Manjurano et al., 2012; Sirugo et al., 2014; Luzzatto, 2015; Manjurano et al., 2015; Uyoga et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Other studies have indicated that the protective effect of G6PD deficiency is present in both heterozygous females and hemizygous males.
source: However other studies have indicated that the protective effect is present in both heterozygous females and hemizygous males (Ruwende et al., 1995; Clark et al., 2009; Shah et al., 2016) or that it is confined to hemizygous G6PD-deficient males (Guindo et al., 2007), or that there are no protective effects at all (Johnson et al., 2009; Toure et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Some studies have indicated that the protective effect of G6PD deficiency is confined to hemizygous G6PD-deficient males.
source: However other studies have indicated that the protective effect is present in both heterozygous females and hemizygous males (Ruwende et al., 1995; Clark et al., 2009; Shah et al., 2016) or that it is confined to hemizygous G6PD-deficient males (Guindo et al., 2007), or that there are no protective effects at all (Johnson et al., 2009; Toure et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Some studies have indicated that there are no protective effects of G6PD deficiency at all.
source: However other studies have indicated that the protective effect is present in both heterozygous females and hemizygous males (Ruwende et al., 1995; Clark et al., 2009; Shah et al., 2016) or that it is confined to hemizygous G6PD-deficient males (Guindo et al., 2007), or that there are no protective effects at all (Johnson et al., 2009; Toure et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Both female heterozygotes and male hemizygotes for the main African form of G6PD deficiency (rs1050828) had reduced risk of cerebral malaria.
source: It was found that both female heterozygotes and male hemizygotes for the main African form of G6PD deficiency (encoded by the derived allele of rs1050828 (G6PD c.202C>T)) had reduced risk of cerebral malaria, but this benefit was offset by increased risk of severe malarial anaemia in male hemizygotes and female homozygotes.
evidence: This is a finding from a previous multi-centre case-control study cited in the manuscript.

claim: Male hemizygotes and female homozygotes for the main African form of G6PD deficiency (rs1050828) had increased risk of severe malarial anaemia.
source: It was found that both female heterozygotes and male hemizygotes for the main African form of G6PD deficiency (encoded by the derived allele of rs1050828 (G6PD c.202C>T)) had reduced risk of cerebral malaria, but this benefit was offset by increased risk of severe malarial anaemia in male hemizygotes and female homozygotes.
evidence: This is a finding from a previous multi-centre case-control study cited in the manuscript.

claim: Sickle cell trait and blood group O were very strongly associated with reduced risk of both cerebral malaria and severe malarial anaemia.
source: By contrast, the sickle cell trait and blood group O were very strongly associated with reduced risk of both cerebral malaria and severe malarial anaemia in the same samples. (Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network, 2014, 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: G6PD deficiency appears to have a more complex mode of action than other malaria-resistance factors.
source: G6PD deficiency thus appears to have a more complex mode of action than other malaria-resistance factors, reducing the risk of some life-threatening complications of P. falciparum infection, but increasing the risk of others.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of G6PD deficiency effects with those of sickle cell trait and blood group O.

claim: G6PD+202T was associated with an increased risk of severe malarial anaemia (odds ratio = 1.18, p = 7.5x10−5) in males and females combined under an additive genetic model.
source: As reported previously (Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network, 2014), G6PD+202T was associated with an increased risk of severe malarial anaemia (odds ratio [OR] = 1.18, p = 7.5x10−5) and a decreased risk of cerebral malaria (OR = 0.91, p = 7.2x10−3) in males and females combined under an additive genetic model (Table 3 and Supplementary files 1D–F).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by statistical analysis presented in Table 3.

claim: G6PD+202T was associated with a decreased risk of cerebral malaria (odds ratio = 0.91, p = 7.2x10−3) in males and females combined under an additive genetic model.
source: As reported previously (Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network, 2014), G6PD+202T was associated with an increased risk of severe malarial anaemia (odds ratio [OR] = 1.18, p = 7.5x10−5) and a decreased risk of cerebral malaria (OR = 0.91, p = 7.2x10−3) in males and females combined under an additive genetic model (Table 3 and Supplementary files 1D–F).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by statistical analysis presented in Table 3.

claim: Six variants other than G6PD+202 showed evidence of association with severe malarial anaemia (p<1x10−3) but they were all in linkage disequilibrium with G6PD+202.
source: Six variants other than G6PD+202 showed evidence of association with severe malarial anaemia (p<1x10−3) but they were all in linkage disequilibrium with G6PD+202 and these associations disappeared after adjusting for the known effects of G6PD+202 (Figure 1, Table 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The associations of six variants other than G6PD+202 with severe malarial anaemia disappeared after adjusting for the known effects of G6PD+202.
source: Six variants other than G6PD+202 showed evidence of association with severe malarial anaemia (p<1x10−3) but they were all in linkage disequilibrium with G6PD+202 and these associations disappeared after adjusting for the known effects of G6PD+202 (Figure 1, Table 4).

claim: There was no evidence that HbC variant, ABO, ATP2B4, and FREM3/GYPE loci affected the association of G6PD variants with severe malaria.
source: We also examined the HbC variant, and the ABO, ATP2B4, and FREM3/GYPE loci, which have well-validated protective effects against severe malaria (Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network, 2014, 2015) and found no evidence that they affected the association of G6PD variants with severe malaria (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Recent analyses at individual study sites have shown no evidence of interaction between the malaria-protective effects of G6PD deficiency and α thalassemia.
source: The available data did not allow us to analyse α thalassemia across all study sites, but recent analyses at individual study sites have shown no evidence of interaction between the malaria-protective effects of G6PD deficiency and α thalassemia (Manjurano et al., 2015; Uyoga et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

source: The mean G6PDd score was 13.5% in controls, 13% in cerebral malaria cases and 16.9% in severe malarial anaemia cases (Supplementary file 1J).

claim: Individuals with very high G6PDd score showed the strongest level of protection against cerebral malaria (OR = 0.28, p = 0.03).
source: Individuals with very high G6PDd score showed the strongest level of protection against cerebral malaria (OR = 0.28, p = 0.03) and an increased risk of severe malarial anaemia (OR = 1.44, p = 0.36), although the latter was not significant due to the smaller sample numbers (Table 6 and Figure 2).

source: In this statistical model, each 10% increase in the G6PDd score decreased the risk of cerebral malaria by approximately 4% (OR = 0.96, p = 5.6x10−5) and increased the risk of severe malarial anaemia by approximately 5% (OR = 1.05, p = 1.4x10−4) (Supplementary file 1J).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Each 10% increase in the G6PDd score increased the risk of severe malarial anaemia by approximately 5% (OR = 1.05, p = 1.4x10−4).

claim: The effect of G6PDd score on cerebral malaria appeared to be the same for males (OR = 0.96, p = 1.6x10−3) and females (OR = 0.96, p = 1.4x10−2).

claim: The effect of G6PDd score on severe malarial anaemia was more pronounced for males (OR = 1.05, p = 1.8x10−4) than for females (OR = 1.03, p = 0.12).

claim: Several lines of evidence indicate that the G6PD+202T allele has been under recent positive selection.

evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: The antimalarial drug primaquine can precipitate severe and sometimes fatal haemolytic anaemia in G6PD-deficient individuals.
source: The antimalarial drug primaquine, which is of great practical importance for the treatment and elimination of P. vivax malaria, can precipitate severe and sometimes fatal haemolytic anaemia in G6PD-deficient individuals (Chu and White, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the literature.

source: In this model, G6PD deficiency was positively selected and rose to an equilibrium value as long as >27% of the severe malaria cases were due to cerebral malaria.
evidence: This is a finding from the evolutionary modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: If the baseline risk of death due to severe malarial anaemia is half that of cerebral malaria, the equilibrium frequency of G6PD+202T is approximately 28%.
source: When the baseline risk of death due to severe malarial anaemia is half that of cerebral malaria, the equilibrium frequency of G6PD+202T, where the number of lives saved equals the number of lives lost, is approximately 28%; whereas at lower allele frequencies, there are more lives saved than lost, and at higher allele frequencies, there are more lives lost than saved (solid red and solid blue lines Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the epidemiological modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: The equilibrium frequency of 28% for G6PD+202T is consistent with G6PD+202T allele frequencies observed in the African populations studied, which ranged from 11% in Cameroon to 28% in Nigeria (excluding The Gambia where there are other deficiency alleles).
source: This is consistent with the 18% median allele frequency that we observe in African populations where G6PD+202T is the only major deficiency allele.
evidence: This is a comparison of the model prediction with observed data.

claim: Severe childhood anaemia in the tropics is often the result of a combination of factors that include malaria, G6PD deficiency, hookworm, micronutrient deficiency, haemoglobinopathies and other infectious diseases.
source: Severe childhood anaemia in the tropics is often the result of a combination of factors that include malaria, G6PD deficiency, hookworm, micronutrient deficiency, haemoglobinopathies and other infectious diseases (Calis et al., 2008; van Hensbroek et al., 2011; Silverberg, 2012; Kassebaum et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: The present findings indicate the need for a new formulation of the balancing-selection hypothesis, in which G6PD polymorphism is maintained in human populations, at least in part, by an evolutionary trade-off between different adverse outcomes of P. falciparum infection.
source: With these caveats, the present findings indicate the need for a new formulation of the balancing-selection hypothesis, in which G6PD polymorphism is maintained in human populations, at least in part, by an evolutionary trade-off between different adverse outcomes of P. falciparum infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings and modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: In both age groups (<2 years and 2–6 years), assuming an additive genetic model, the G6PD+202T allele was associated with reduced risk of cerebral malaria.
